doc_level_notes: Central argument: the study asks whether industries spend differently on politics when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow. Two opposing mechanisms are kept open: better performance supplies more money, or weak performance or a weak forecast prompts spending to seek favorable policy. The sign is left to estimation.

Two kinds of forecast are kept distinct: predicted industry growth is the independent variable of direct interest (C3, L3), while predicted congressional control is a political control and a predictor of partisan direction.

Six core tests: contributions (C1 prior actual growth, C2 same-year actual growth, C3 predicted growth) and lobbying (L1, L2, L3). Actual-growth tests are associations. C3 and L3 are the tests that address the forecast directly. All six must be reported, including null, negative and inconclusive results.

Design: pooled multiple OLS with sector fixed effects, outcomes in millions of 2025 dollars, growth in percentage points. The plan argues pooling gives more information than fitting about 18 annual observations per sector separately, and it treats simple regression only as an illustration.

Extensions are kept separate: job-tier differences (Chief, Middle Management, Employee reference, with growth-by-tier interactions), chamber-specific Democratic share models, prior plus predicted growth together, and a logged-spending sensitivity check. Zero and negative net totals must not be dropped to make logs work.

Stated epistemic limits: the forecasts proxy public expectations, not firms' private expectations or whether a donor read the report. Results are to be read as associations consistent with a response to public forecasts, not causation. Effect size, uncertainty and consistency take priority over p-values.

Stated readiness gap: verified contribution years overlap the prepared congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, which is too little annual variation to identify the full control specification. Earlier contributions and/or extended congressional forecasts are needed before the core models can be fitted. Adding sectors or tiers does not fix this.

Other gaps the plan names: life insurance, auto, Credit Arms, P&C and Telecom lobbying totals still need classification; Fintech lacks a comparable annual series; crypto has one verified forecast; Telecom wired, ISP and satellite archives are uncollected; the 2008 auto and life-insurance lagged-growth observations are incomplete.

Internal consistency items noticed while reading: Section 6A has spacing corruption ('yielded63', 'forecasts2008-2025', 'with2024 flagged'); counts are stated in several places (63/53/86 strict inputs, 72 original reports in the expansion, 162-row expanded scaffold, 72-row original table) and should be reconciled before reporting; the forecast coding for Democratic control is 1 minus P(R) while the actual-control coding is 1 for Democratic.

doc_level_notes: Mismatch: the file read in full is a methodology note on measuring IBISWorld industry revenue, not a literature annotation document. No cited works, takeaways, or cross-references exist to extract, so no entries were produced.

Claim 1 of the note: IBISWorld Key Statistics dollar figures, including forecasts, are already inflation-adjusted constant-price values, with the base year equal to the report's publication year (U.S. Industry Reports use the BEA implicit GDP price deflator). The 2026 report vintages therefore express revenue in constant 2026 U.S. dollars.

Claim 2: 2006-2025 exports from 2026 vintages should be treated as IBISWorld historical estimates in a common price base, not raw or nominal revenue. Industry definition, publication date and report source must travel with each export. The 2026 row is excluded because IBISWorld says current-year revenue mixes forecasts and current-year ratios.

Method: annual real growth is growth_t_pct = 100 * (R_t / R_(t-1) - 1), applied directly to published values with no CPI ratio or further deflator. Rebasing all observations by one constant leaves growth unchanged. CPI conversion applies only to nominal political-spending amounts.
Lag structure: 2006 is kept as baseline so 2007 growth exists as the one-year-lagged predictor for study year 2008, i.e. 100 * (R_2007 / R_2006 - 1).

Stated gap and exception: February 2008 auto reports use a shared 2006 basis, inferred from equal current and constant-price 2006 rows. The publication-year rule must not overwrite that older evidence; each original vintage keeps its own basis. Details are deferred to price_basis_recheck.md, which was not opened here because it was outside the named target.

Sources cited in the note (as written): IBISWorld Glossary, Constant prices (help.ibisworld.com/en/articles/8156094-glossary); IBISWorld Sourcing and Methodology FAQs (help.ibisworld.com/en/articles/9421472-sourcing-and-methodology-faqs). These are the note's own citations, not verified here. A report-specific units note overrides the general rule if it states a different price basis.

Document: "Predicted industry growth: collected data" (sha12 97fccd058a3f), prepared September 25, 2026 for Paul Goff. It is a data-collection memo for a predicted-growth input to a political-spending study, not an annotated literature review. The source file is C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\97fccd058a3f.txt (read in full, 88 lines). No file in C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\ is named for this sha, and a content search of that folder found no reference to 97fccd058a3f. So there are no reviewer comments or highlights, and no annotation-derived takeaways exist. The entries below cover the works and sources the memo cites. Their takeaways are the memo's own claims, paraphrased, and each verbatim_anchor is the exact opening of the cited passage, not an annotation.

Overarching argument: a sector's predicted real growth, taken from an original-vintage IBISWorld forecast, is a candidate predictor of that sector's political spending (contributions and lobbying) in the following year. The forecast is built so its baseline and forecast come from the same report, published in the preceding calendar year, which avoids using revised later data. Election timing and expected congressional control are treated as conditioning factors. The memo states the predicted-growth regressions should run separately from the four actual-growth regressions in the research plan. Contributions can then be split across Chief, Middle Management and Employee tiers.

Research questions and rules set out: which forecast values are usable in the main real-growth column versus the broader collected column; how to treat price-basis uncertainty (IBISWorld real-growth values get no second CPI adjustment, while CPI still converts nominal spending to 2025 dollars); and blank means missing or unresolved, never zero.

Syntheses across works: the 2008–2025 five-sector grid (90 rows) and the four-sector joined table (72 rows) both use unique sector-year keys. The auto series combines two component reports (cars 33611a and SUVs/light trucks 33611b) for 2011–2012 by adding revenue levels first, not averaging growth rates, and the memo flags continuity with the merged 33611 code as an explicit assumption to check by excluding those rows. Crypto (Statista, -3.78%) is kept as a separate proxy because its scope and inflation basis differ from the IBISWorld series.

Stated gaps: life insurance 2008–2010 forecast targets are missing (the 2007 edition covers life, health and medical together and is excluded; no 2008 or 2009 edition was listed); auto 2009–2010 lack a common component price base; 2024 auto price basis is unverified; two IBISWorld values (credit union 2024 was later cleared; life and auto December 2023 remain flagged) are held out of the main column; the retired-code archive pages list 2012–2022 publication years but did not render downloadable reports; the acquisition is partial, not exhaustive (the recheck adds 12 supplemental observations). Outstanding work: spending extraction and congressional-forecast coverage per the research plan. No regressions have been run. The memo explicitly says that obtaining these forecasts does not resolve those coverage limits.

No Melange, Moneyball, Mentat or Terrier components are named in this document. The only system link stated is the political-spending study and its research plan.

doc_level_notes: Research question: does sector real industry growth, measured same-year (k=0) and previous-year (k=1), predict political spending, separately for contributions and lobbying, after controlling for presidential and midterm years and expected Democratic House and Senate control (lines 42-54). Two predicted-growth tests are added, for six core regressions in total (line 56).

Direction question: party direction is measured as Democratic share of House or Senate contributions, with missing values where the denominator is zero (line 58). A total-dollar outcome alone cannot answer the direction question.

Job-level split: contributions are kept at sector x year x tier (Chief, Middle Management, Employee), with organizational and PAC giving separate. Lobbying has no equivalent split in the verified sources (line 60). The Employee tier includes unrecognized-title fallbacks, so it is not purely verified rank-and-file.

Methodological stance: blank values stay missing. Absent forecasts, uncovered sectors and incomplete years must not become zero spending or zero probability (line 32). Expectations variables are concurrent controls, not proof that expectations cause spending (line 77). Coefficients absorb the cycle, and no fixed presidential-to-midterm ratio is assumed (line 54).

Forecast construction: the archive's House and Senate forecasts used different denominators. The rebuilt conditional file uses one D/R denominator for both chambers, conditioned on neither chamber landing in the OTHER outcome (lines 18, 77). The annual means use only dates before the targeted election, not the full year.

Stated gaps: no matching crypto revenue series; life-insurance and auto need 2006 revenue for the 2008 lagged observation; no verified pre-2021 contribution corpus in the scoped local search (the document says this does not prove absence elsewhere); lobbying not yet aligned to research sectors; life-insurance and auto lobbying not in the cached outputs; 2023 to 2025 forecast controls absent (line 18).

Scope and category mismatch: the existing Mentat categories do not cover the research sector set. P&C insurance is not a substitute for life insurance, and fintech is not a substitute for crypto (line 22). Pull-through to the spending panel therefore depends on sector matching that is not done.

Internal count inconsistencies that the document does not reconcile: line 3 cites 72 original reports and 86 strict annual growth inputs for the nine-sector expansion; line 7 cites 55 IBISWorld sector-year values, 53 of which pass; line 26 describes the combined table as 72 rows across four matched sectors; line 15 lists four captured sectors. These may be different scopes (nine-sector expansion versus four core sectors), but the document does not say so explicitly.

Scope note: the document is a sector growth and political spending study. It does not discuss Melange path-finding, social-network analysis, allocation, Moneyball scoring, Mentat or Terrier as literature, and it contains no literature annotations about those systems. Systems appear only as data sources (Melange spending records, Mentat receipts and tiers).

Document read in full: C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\f8366afe89c8.txt (sha12 f8366afe89c8), titled "Speech Cuts, Turns, and Audio: Corpus and Accuracy Status," as of 2026-08-29. The annotation file C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\f8366afe89c8.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights.

This is an internal status report on the speech-recognition lane that feeds the Big Five personality work in the Moneyball model. It is not a literature annotation. It cites no external published works, so no bibliographic entries are extracted. Its sources are internal Melange files (big5_methods.md, several big5_*_prereg.md files, fec/collect/fetch_hearings_seq.py, b5_audio_verify.py, b5_audio_build.py, b5_speech_quirks.py, an audit folder), and Melange project brain items (D-013, DE-008, DE-009, the anchor-pad constraint).

Overarching argument: the capture pipeline works. Anchor-based capture (a stimulus anchor pad plus manifest offset, and on-screen chyron, and caption text) pins each member's turn exactly (751/751 offsets; padded/unpadded cross-correlation about 1.000 at median lag 20.00s). That yields a ~161-hour, 448-member voice corpus and a 532-of-533-member speech text corpus of about 57.6M words. Transcription (Gemini plus a pinned local Whisper producer) agrees with YouTube captions at 0.945 mean word coverage (n=30 windows), but this is reference-dependent: 0.745 against condensed C-SPAN text, and no human-gold WER exists yet.

Main synthesis: every attempt to validate audio as a Big Five measurement channel missed, was redundant with text, or was confounded. ES held-out r=+0.208 vanished after controls (partial r=-0.029 after gender and party, since pitch encodes speaker sex). E audio-alone r=+0.228 sat inside the permutation noise floor. The N prereg look missed on all four bars (r=-0.0016, n=110), and the channels appear to carry C/E-flavoured signal rather than N. The one partial positive (Pink-E r=+0.284, ES r=+0.298) cannot yield per-trait claims because audio A and ES are halo-inseparable (|r|=0.819). The ruling of record (D-013, 2026-08-25) pivots audio to descriptive, display-only measurement (triggers, speech-habit signatures, agreement/disagreement) with no engine wiring and no trait-validity claims without a fresh locked prereg.

Reliability and venue findings: quirk rates (Spearman-Brown 0.794), pause behavior (0.799 NPR; 0.882 Sunday shows), volume dynamics (0.708) and pitch variability (0.707) clear the 0.70 bar at 5 units. Floor-speech prosody, F0 slopes and vocal strain do not. Filler rates differ roughly 100x between live Washington Journal (~26 per 1k words) and NPR (0.22 per 1k), so raw cross-venue comparisons are invalid.

Stated gaps and open items (all Paul's calls): rebuild hearings_seq.db to fix the 9.7% (65,912) cross-chamber mis-attribution defect, since the code fix of 2026-08-18 is not yet in the database feeding the desk and antagonism scoring; re-adjudicate 33.7% of kept audio clips lacking identifying content; run the 150-clip human-gold annotation packet to get a real WER; and register two speech test suites (test_cspan_identity.py, test_big5_gold_audio_tdd.py) in a runner, since their production guard currently passes vacuously. The document also notes that identity-from-voice alone was tested once (0/7) and acoustic speaker verification was closed (best EER 0.226), so identity must come from anchors and text, with voice used only as a veto.

Research questions implicit in the text: whether audio carries a stable, independent per-member trait signal (answered mostly negative so far), and whether speech habits are reliable enough to describe members (answered yes for a subset of measures, with venue-specific caveats).
